intro: A low B, two harps and the soft roll of timpani open La Mer; by noon, horns and trombones are singing a chorale. Paul Paray conducts the Detroit Symphony Orchestra.

sections.label: Intro · Low strings, harps and timpani
sections.mNote: The first phrases emerge above a low B

sections.label: A · D♭ major, running strings
sections.mNote: Short wind phrases ride over quick string figures

sections.label: B · Sixteen cellos in four parts
sections.mNote: The cellos unfold a long, strongly rhythmic tune

sections.label: Coda · The noon chorale
sections.mNote: Horns and trombones broaden the tune above flowing harps

cues.title: Dawn on B
cues.text: Double basses and timpani hold a low B. The two harps answer one another; muted cellos and violas begin to move above them. Debussy writes Très lent — very slow. The violins wait.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, opening, printed p. 143: timpani and divided basses on B, alternating harps, then muted cellos and violas. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/b6/IMSLP15420-Debussy_-_La_Mer_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sea from Burgundy
cues.text: Debussy begins La Mer in the summer of 1903, while staying with his parents-in-law in Burgundy. The sea is far away. He has the memory of childhood holidays at Cannes, and the score grows from there.
cues.evidence: Composition in Burgundy: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy). Childhood visits to Cannes: Jacob Greenberg’s Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer

cues.title: D♭ begins to flow
cues.text: The main movement changes to D♭ major and 6/8, marked Modéré, sans lenteur — moderate, without slowness. Divided strings keep the semiquavers running while the woodwinds pass short phrases between them.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 147–150: 6/8 and five flats, moving divided strings and wind phrases.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two against three
cues.text: Twos and threes keep crossing in this movement. One part divides the beat into triplets while another plays even notes. The harps and divided strings can be busy with several rhythms beneath a single wind phrase.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg describes the persistent interplay of duplets and triplets in movement I: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer. Examples appear throughout the Durand score.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Sixteen cellos
cues.text: Debussy asks for sixteen cellos, divided into four groups. They sing a new tune in interlocking parts, with the horns answering above them. Très rythmé, he writes: the long melody still has a spring in its step.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, rehearsal 9, printed p. 161: sixteen cellos divided into four parts, Très rythmé, with horn replies.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hokusai’s wave
cues.text: Debussy chooses Hokusai’s The Great Wave off Kanagawa for the cover of the published score. The Japanese print is cropped and redrawn for Durand’s 1905 edition.
cues.evidence: Debussy’s choice of the Hokusai image: Jacob Greenberg, https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer; the first-edition cover is reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy).

cues.title: Horns, trombones, noon
cues.text: Très lent again. Bassoons, horns and trombones sing the chorale, with triplets in the flutes and flowing harp figures below. The music is broad without standing still. Its final chords bring D♭ major into full daylight.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, rehearsal 14 to the end of movement I, printed pp. 171–173: Très lent, bassoon and brass chorale, flute triplets, harps and D♭-major ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: B opens into D♭
transitions.from: Intro · Low strings, harps and timpani
transitions.how: The introduction accelerates into Modéré, sans lenteur. B-centred harmony opens into D♭ major, and 6/4 becomes 6/8. The bassoons and harps punctuate the change while divided second violins and violas set the semiquavers running.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 146–147, the end of the introduction and opening of the main 6/8.

transitions.title: The cellos take four parts
transitions.to: B · Sixteen cellos in four parts
transitions.how: The preceding chords subside into quiet timpani and strings. At Très rythmé, sixteen cellos divide into four parts, their tune rising over plucked double basses. Horn calls answer the cello phrases; the high woodwinds fall silent.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 160–161, leading into rehearsal 9. The established section boundary places this passage.

transitions.title: The brass opens out
transitions.from: B · Sixteen cellos in four parts
transitions.how: The quiet cor anglais and cello phrases lead to Très lent. Bassoons, horns and trombones take up the chorale above a low D♭. Harps keep moving beneath them, and the flutes play triplets. A crescendo carries this hushed opening to the full-orchestra D♭-major close.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 170–173, including rehearsal 14, Très lent.

source.title: Debussy, La Mer · Durand full score, plates D. & F. 6532 / 6838
source.locator: Movement I, printed pp. 143–173: the low-string introduction, divided strings at Modéré, sans lenteur, and the brass chorale at rehearsal 14.

timeline.note: Muted lower strings, quiet timpani and harps begin over a low B.
Cor anglais and muted trumpet trade short calls above the low strings.
Divided second violins and violas run in semiquavers beneath the wind phrases.
Bassoons, horns and trombones sustain the slow chorale while flutes and harps keep moving.
The full orchestra gathers around D♭ major, ending with short, emphatic chords.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
